say.text: Time to read the tracings. Picture the right ventricle (RV) pumping against a narrowed outflow, with a hole in the septum letting it empty into the aorta.
Predict: what does the ECG show?

choices.label: Left axis deviation with a left ventricular hypertrophy pattern
Right axis deviation with a right ventricular hypertrophy pattern
Left atrial enlargement with left ventricular hypertrophy
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which chamber carries the extra load here. The ECG records the chamber that is working hardest, so name that chamber first.
Left-sided changes are tempting because a VSD sounds like a left-heart problem and LVH is the textbook 'big heart' pattern.
But here the load sits on the right: the ECG shows right axis deviation and prominent R waves in V1, a right ventricular and right atrial pattern.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: in TOF the ECG follows the RV, which is the chamber under pressure.

say.text: Left atrial enlargement with LVH feels natural if you carry over the left-sided shunt picture.
TOF reads the other way round: the ECG is characteristic of right atrial enlargement and right ventricular hypertrophy, with right axis deviation.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pause here: every change on the TOF ECG points right, not left.

say.text: Observe what the tracing shows: right axis deviation, prominent R or qR waves in V1 and upright T waves in V1, characteristic of right atrial enlargement and right ventricular hypertrophy.

choices.label: Why does it look like that?

say.text: Now explain it. Why is there a right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH) pattern at all?

choices.label: VSD volume overloads the left ventricle and strains the right
The RV is thick as a primary malformation, present before any load
The RV works against chronic systemic-level pressure, so it thickens

say.text: Yes. RVH is secondary to chronic systemic pressures; it sits at the end of the chain, after the septal malalignment and the infundibular narrowing.
Volume overload of the left side is a familiar shunt idea, so it is tempting.
The bank gives a different mechanism: RVH is secondary to chronic systemic pressures on the RV, a pressure load rather than a left-sided volume load.
Calling RVH a defect is tempting because it is one of the four named components.
But it is the component that develops last: RVH is secondary to chronic systemic pressures, a consequence rather than a primary malformation.
Next, the chest X-ray. Follow the blood: with significant RVOT obstruction, where does it go?
Predict the lung fields.

choices.label: Plethoric: the VSD floods the lungs
Normal lung fields, but marked cardiomegaly
Oligaemic: blood bypasses the pulmonary bed

say.text: Observe: with significant RVOT obstruction, most of the blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed, so the film can show decreased pulmonary vascular markings (pulmonary oligaemia).
StatPearls also describes a normal-size heart silhouette.
Plethora is tempting because a VSD alone sends blood left to right and floods the lungs.
In TOF the obstruction redirects most blood toward the aorta, bypassing the lungs, so markings decrease (oligaemia).
Normal lungs with a big heart is tempting if you picture a failing, dilated heart.
The film shows decreased pulmonary markings, and StatPearls describes a normal-size heart silhouette.
One more film feature: the classic 'boot' has an upturned apex.
Predict: what lifts the apex?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The ECG just told you which ventricle is thick in TOF. Which one would shape the apex?
Yes. The upturned apex is attributed to RVH, together with a concave pulmonary arterial segment.
Mind the wording: chest radiographs may classically show a boot-shaped heart. It is a 'may classically' sign, not a certainty.
A big pulmonary artery is tempting because the boot is linked to the pulmonary segment.
The segment is concave, not dilated, and the upturned apex is attributed to RVH.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again: a concave segment is the opposite of a dilated one.

say.text: LVH is tempting because the left ventricle is the apex-forming chamber in a normal heart.
In TOF the upturned apex is attributed to right ventricular hypertrophy.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: the thick ventricle in TOF is the right one.

say.text: Put the pieces together. Which description fits the TOF chest X-ray?

choices.label: Normal-sized heart, upturned apex, oligaemic lung fields
Egg-on-a-string heart with a narrow pedicle

say.text: Yes: a normal-size silhouette with an upturned apex (K31), and decreased pulmonary markings from blood bypassing the lungs.
Cardiomegaly with plethora is the picture of a left-to-right flood, so it is tempting.
The TOF film instead has a normal-size heart silhouette and decreased pulmonary markings.
A named, memorable silhouette like this is tempting as a look-alike for the boot.
I can only vouch for the TOF film: a normal-size silhouette with an upturned apex and a concave main pulmonary artery segment, with oligaemic lungs.
A cyanotic 2-month-old has a harsh murmur at the left upper sternal border and right axis deviation on ECG.
Which test confirms TOF?

choices.label: Chest X-ray looking for a boot-shaped heart
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think of the test that lets you see the abnormal anatomy directly, without relying on a sign that may or may not be there.
Yes. Echocardiography is the gold standard and primary diagnostic modality; it allows direct visualisation of the abnormal anatomy.
The boot shape is the best-known TOF film sign, so it is tempting to call it confirmatory.
But radiographs only may classically show it. The test that confirms is echocardiography, the gold standard.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again: a 'may classically' sign cannot be the confirming test.

say.text: Catheterisation feels like the definitive, invasive test, so it is tempting as 'gold standard'.
For diagnosis, the bank names echocardiography as the gold standard and primary modality, with direct visualisation of the anatomy.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth fixing: echo, not catheterisation, is the gold standard for diagnosis.

say.text: Echo has confirmed TOF. Before repair, the team wants the complex cardiovascular morphology shown in detail.
Which test adds this?
Yes. Contrast-enhanced CT is useful in demonstrating the complex cardiovascular morphology of TOF.

choices.label: Why not echo alone? Go deeper

say.text: Echo is the gold standard, so it is tempting to think it covers everything.
It is the diagnostic test, but contrast-enhanced CT is the one cited for demonstrating the complex cardiovascular morphology.
Catheterisation sounds like the most detailed test, so it is tempting.
The gold standard for diagnosis is echo; the test cited for complex morphology is contrast-enhanced CT.
Echocardiography has limitations in assessing associated extracardiac anomalies, such as peripheral pulmonary stenosis and atresia.
Detailed pulmonary artery assessment matters: repairing the cardiac defects without addressing pulmonary artery hypoplasia or stenosis has a poor outcome.
Last rung. Which pairing of test and job is right in TOF?

choices.label: Echo for diagnosis; MRI for anatomy plus function without radiation
MRI for first-line diagnosis; echo for follow-up only
Catheterisation for diagnosis; echo for screening only

say.text: Yes. MRI provides both anatomical detail and functional information without ionising radiation, while echo remains the primary diagnostic modality.
MRI's detail and lack of radiation make it tempting as first line.
Echo remains the primary modality for diagnosis; MRI adds anatomical detail and function without ionising radiation.
